title: Flask Setup
text: Flask Setup How AIWAF works: system architecture Add AIWAF to a Flask application and verify that protection is registered with the live route table. Before you begin Use an environment compatible with your framework. This guide assumes a Python application file named app.py. New to middleware? Start with the six-step first protected app tutorial , which includes complete files and expected responses. 1. Install the framework extra pip install "aiwaf[flask]" pip install "aiwaf[rust]" # optional native acceleration Install into the environment used to run your application. Choose an interpreter compatible with the framework and dependencies. 2. Register protection app.py from flask import Flask from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF app = Flask(__name__) AIWAF( app, middlewares=["auto"], ) @app.get("/") def home(): return {"protected": True} middlewares=["all"] enables the canonical middleware set. auto starts from the same set and omits checks that are not useful for the detected application signals. 3. Discover your live routes Run from the application checkout after all routes are registered: aiwaf init --framework flask --app app:app For a file named app.py containing app = Flask(__name__) , use --app app:app , not --app app.py . The first part is the Python module name without .py ; the second is the application object. Run the command from the directory containing app.py . The CLI imports your application, so its dependencies and configuration must be available. The default output is .aiwaf/paths.json . Flask and FastAPI require module:object in --app ; Flask factories such as app:create_app are supported. Repeat discovery when registered routes change. 4. Scope route exemptions Django, Flask, and FastAPI expose equivalent route helpers: from aiwaf.flask import ( aiwaf_exempt, aiwaf_exempt_from, aiwaf_only, aiwaf_require_protection, ) @app.get("/health") @aiwaf_exempt def health(): return {"ok": True} @app.post("/webhook") @aiwaf_only("header_validation") def webhook(): return {"accepted": True} Canonical middleware names include header_validation , rate_limit , ip_keyword_block , honeypot , geo_block , uuid_tamper , ai_anomaly , and logging . 5. Configure settings and model storage Set flat AIWAF_* values in app.config before calling AIWAF(app) . Flask's constructor selects middleware; it does not accept FastAPI's nested option dictionaries. Area Important settings Training AIWAF_ACCESS_LOG , AIWAF_MIN_TRAIN_LOGS , AIWAF_MIN_AI_LOGS , AIWAF_FORCE_AI_TRAINING Rate limiting AIWAF_RATE_WINDOW , AIWAF_RATE_MAX , AIWAF_RATE_FLOOD Headers AIWAF_REQUIRED_HEADERS , AIWAF_HEADER_QUALITY_MIN_SCORE Honeypot AIWAF_MIN_FORM_TIME , AIWAF_MAX_PAGE_TIME UUID checks AIWAF_UUID_SCORE_ENABLED , AIWAF_UUID_SCORE_BLOCK_THRESHOLD GeoIP AIWAF_GEO_BLOCK_ENABLED , AIWAF_GEO_BLOCK_COUNTRIES , AIWAF_GEO_ALLOW_COUNTRIES Exemptions AIWAF_EXEMPT_PATHS , AIWAF_EXEMPT_KEYWORDS , AIWAF_ALLOWED_PATH_KEYWORDS Models AIWAF_MODEL_PATH , AIWAF_MODEL_STORAGE , AIWAF_MODEL_STORAGE_FALLBACK When aiwaf_rust is importable, supported acceleration paths are selected automatically. Python remains the fallback when a native capability is unavailable. Persisted runtime models use JSON state; AIWAF does not load pickle, joblib, or other executable Python-object formats. 6. Start and verify python -m flask --app app:app run --port 5000 Open http://127.0.0.1:5000/ in a browser. The handler should return {"protected": true} . Also test a deliberately rejected request on a non-exempt route; success alone does not prove enforcement. For exact three-success/one-throttle behavior, use the tutorial's controlled rate-limit test . aiwaf flask --help aiwaf flask train --help aiwaf flask model --help Use Python operations for training, model inspection, and state migration. Training requires representative logs in a supported format; setup alone does not train a model. Production configuration Configure the application to trust forwarding headers only from known proxy CIDRs. Configure the outermost proxy to overwrite client-supplied forwarding headers. Use Redis, a database, or another shared backend when multiple workers must share rate-limit, blacklist, or exemption state. Keep health checks, static assets, and trusted webhook routes explicitly scoped instead of disabling protection globally. Start anomaly detection in observe-only or conservative mode and tune it with representative normal traffic. Rotate logs and exclude secrets, authorization headers, cookies, and personal data. Sign model/configuration artifacts where the runtime supports HMAC verification. Run AIWAF alongside normal secure-development controls and an edge/reverse-proxy layer. Checkpoint You can identify the settings location, import target, registered routes, and verification step for Flask. Choose a runtime Next: understand Python architecture

title: Rust and WebAssembly Accelerators
text: Rust and WebAssembly Accelerators How AIWAF works: system architecture aiwaf-rust and aiwaf-wasm are versioned independently from the Python and Node packages. Both currently declare version 0.2.1 in the local monorepo. They share rust/crates/aiwaf_core/ ; PyO3 bindings live in rust/src/lib.rs , and WASM bindings in rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm/ . Python bindings aiwaf-rust exposes the shared Rust core through PyO3 and ABI3 wheels for Python 3.8 and newer. pip install aiwaf-rust The module provides: validate_headers and validate_headers_with_config KeywordMatcher and RouteMatcher request-record construction and six-feature extraction incremental feature extraction with explicit state recent-behavior analysis IsolationForest training, scoring, prediction, retraining, and JSON state import aiwaf_rust reason = aiwaf_rust.validate_headers({ "HTTP_USER_AGENT": "Mozilla/5.0", "HTTP_ACCEPT": "text/html", }) forest = aiwaf_rust.IsolationForest( n_estimators=100, max_samples="auto", contamination="auto", max_features=1.0, bootstrap=False, random_state=42, warm_start=False, ) forest.fit([[0.1, 1.0], [0.2, 1.1], [9.0, 9.0]]) score = forest.anomaly_score([9.0, 9.0]) state = forest.to_json() restored = aiwaf_rust.IsolationForest.from_json(state) For a local native build, stage the two canonical repository assets and run maturin: cp README.md rust/README.md cp LICENSE rust/LICENSE cp NOTICE rust/NOTICE cp -R licenses rust/ python -m pip install maturin cd rust maturin develop The staged files are ignored by Git. Release automation performs the same staging before building wheels and the source distribution. WebAssembly bindings aiwaf-wasm exposes the shared Rust core to browsers and Node-compatible bundlers. import init, { IsolationForest, KeywordMatcher, RouteMatcher, analyze_recent_behavior, extract_features, validate_headers, } from 'aiwaf-wasm'; await init(); const reason = validate_headers({ 'user-agent': 'Mozilla/5.0', accept: 'text/html' }); const forest = new IsolationForest({ n_estimators: 100, max_samples: 'auto', contamination: 'auto', random_state: 42 }); forest.fit([[0.1, 1.0], [0.2, 1.1], [9.0, 9.0]]); const score = forest.anomaly_score([9.0, 9.0]); The WASM API includes header, URL, and content validation; keyword and route matchers; record conversion; batched feature extraction; recent-behavior analysis; and Isolation Forest lifecycle methods. Browser use requires a bundler that understands WebAssembly assets. Build and test it locally: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --locked -p aiwaf_core cd rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm wasm-pack test --node wasm-pack build --release --target bundler cd ../.. python scripts/patch_wasm_pkg.py cp ../LICENSE crates/aiwaf_wasm/pkg/LICENSE cp ../NOTICE crates/aiwaf_wasm/pkg/NOTICE cp -R ../licenses crates/aiwaf_wasm/pkg/ Continue Binding API and scoring semantics Build, tests, and packaging

title: Rust and WASM Architecture
text: Rust and WASM Architecture Rust implements shared computation primitives. PyO3 and wasm-bindgen expose them to host applications, while the Python or JavaScript host retains responsibility for HTTP policy, storage, logging, and response handling. On this page One core, two binding boundaries Matching without rebuilding work per request Record conversion and stateful feature extraction Inside the forest JSON is the artifact boundary Acceleration has a conversion cost Worked example: accelerated header validation Trace the implementation How AIWAF works: system architecture One core, two binding boundaries Host runtime Select the operation and provide normalized input. Binding conversion PyO3 or wasm-bindgen converts host values into Rust data. Shared Rust core Match, validate, extract features, analyze behavior, or score a forest. Host decision Convert the result back and apply framework policy. Source area Responsibility rust/crates/aiwaf_core/src/lib.rs Shared keyword and route matching, request records, feature windows, behavior analysis, and Isolation Forest state. rust/src/lib.rs PyO3 objects and conversion routines exposed as aiwaf_rust . rust/crates/aiwaf_wasm/src/lib.rs wasm-bindgen exports and JavaScript conversion exposed as aiwaf-wasm . Matching without rebuilding work per request KeywordMatcher escapes configured keywords into literal patterns and builds a regex set. first_match preserves configured keyword order. The host can reuse the matcher rather than rebuilding pattern machinery on each request. RouteMatcher indexes normalized prefixes. Matching starts with the deepest candidate and walks parent path boundaries until it finds a stored prefix. Duplicate normalized prefixes retain their first configured index. The host still normalizes paths and interprets the matching rule's policy. Record conversion and stateful feature extraction Bindings convert request records into typed structures before the core computes features. Batched and incremental extraction share the computation layer; incremental calls carry explicit state so recent client activity is available across batches. That extraction state is distinct from a framework's blacklist or distributed rate-limit store. Sending a batch to Rust does not automatically replicate application state across workers. The host chooses where records and extraction state live. Feature What it describes Why it helps path_len Length of the request path. Unusually long probing paths. kw_hits Matches against malicious keywords. Known probing patterns within a path. resp_time Response duration in seconds. Behavior that differs from the normal timing distribution. status_idx An encoded response-status category. Response outcomes without treating status codes as continuous measurements. burst_count Requests associated with the client in the burst window. Rapid repeated activity. total_404 Not-found responses in the relevant per-client history. Repeated discovery of nonexistent routes. The feature order is part of the model contract. A trainer and scorer must agree on the order, status mapping, time units, and window semantics. Summary fields ending in _ms use milliseconds; the feature vector uses seconds. Sharing feature names alone does not make every model artifact interchangeable. Inside the forest Training samples rows and grows isolation trees with random feature selections and split points. Tree traversal measures the number of splits required to isolate a point; short average isolation paths indicate more unusual samples. anomaly_score uses the direction where higher means more anomalous. score_samples uses the opposite, scikit-learn-aligned direction. decision_function subtracts the configured offset, and predict returns inlier or outlier labels. The host must use the matching threshold convention. Ordinary fitting replaces the forest unless warm-start append is selected. Retraining supports the append lifecycle. Random seeds and sampling settings affect the trained state, so score comparisons should use compatible artifacts and settings. JSON is the artifact boundary The forest exports state through to_json and restores it through from_json . Tree structure, settings, and scoring state travel as data. The host decides whether to store that state in a file, database, or cache and checks feature and artifact compatibility when loading. Python's Rust-model artifact can be exchanged with the supported Java JSON model path. JavaScript-native forests and older artifacts are not automatically the same format just because they use six feature names. Acceleration has a conversion cost Python calls cross the native-extension boundary; JavaScript calls cross the WASM boundary. Converting object-heavy inputs consumes time before the Rust computation starts. Reusing matchers and processing sufficiently large feature batches can amortize that cost. The Python bridge selects installed capabilities and retains fallback behavior. The Node adapter can choose JavaScript when WASM initialization or conversion is unsuitable. A native function returning a suspicious reason still requires the host to turn that result into a policy decision. Worked example: accelerated header validation The Python adapter receives framework headers and normalizes HTTP or WSGI key names. The bridge passes the resulting dictionary and validation options through PyO3. Rust evaluates the configured header rules and returns a reason or a clean result. The Python middleware then decides whether to return a response, record an offense, or continue to the handler. The Rust core never sends the Flask or FastAPI response itself. This boundary explains why framework configuration and exemptions continue to matter when native acceleration is enabled. text: Bindings API PyO3 And WASM Function Reference How AIWAF works: system architecture 5. PyO3 (Python) Binding Functions Header Validation validate_headers(headers: dict) -> Optional[str] validate_headers_with_config(headers: dict, required_headers: Optional[list[str]], min_score: Optional[int]) -> Optional[str] Matchers and record conversion KeywordMatcher(keywords).first_match(path) returns the first matching keyword or None . RouteMatcher(prefixes).match_index(path) returns the matching prefix index or None . Record helpers include build_records , extract_raw_features , and extract_training_features . Feature Extraction extract_features(records: list[dict], static_keywords: list[str]) -> list[dict] extract_features_batch_with_state(records: list[dict], static_keywords: list[str], state: Optional[dict]) -> dict finalize_feature_state(static_keywords: list[str], state: Optional[dict]) -> dict Recent Behavior Analysis analyze_recent_behavior(entries: list[dict], static_keywords: list[str]) -> Optional[dict] IsolationForest (PyO3) Constructor supports n_estimators , max_samples , contamination , max_features , bootstrap , n_jobs (ignored), random_state , verbose , warm_start . Methods: fit , retrain , anomaly_score , is_anomaly , score_samples , decision_function , predict , to_json , from_json . 6. Isolation Forest Internals And Semantics Core implementation in rust/crates/aiwaf_core/src/lib.rs . fit resets trees unless warm-start append is enabled. retrain temporarily forces warm-start append behavior. anomaly_score : higher means more anomalous. score_samples : higher means more normal (sklearn-aligned direction). decision_function = score_samples - offset_ . predict returns 1 (inlier) and -1 (outlier). Contamination "auto" keeps offset_ = -0.5 ; fixed contamination computes percentile-based offset. 7. WASM Binding Functions validate_headers , validate_headers_with_config extract_features , extract_features_batch_with_state , finalize_feature_state analyze_recent_behavior WASM also exports KeywordMatcher , RouteMatcher , validate_url , validate_content , and record-conversion helpers. WASM IsolationForest class new(config?) , fit , retrain , anomaly_score , is_anomaly , score_samples , decision_function , predict , to_json , from_json Header Handling Notes WASM accepts JS object or Headers . Auto-fills user-agent from navigator.userAgent when absent. Core still expects normalized HTTP_* style names internally. 8. Integration Patterns Python service pattern Build normalized request dict. Run header validation early; block on non- None reason. Build feature records and update state incrementally. Score with IsolationForest and combine with rule outcomes. JS/browser WASM pattern await init() at startup. Use wasm exports in request/event pipeline. Persist forest/state with to_json() as needed. Python ↔ WASM portability Both bindings expose JSON state from the shared Rust core. Validate the serialized feature schema and forest version before exchanging artifacts. Java supports Python Rust-model JSON state; JavaScript-native and legacy artifacts are not generally interchangeable.

title: Operations and troubleshooting
text: How-to guide Operations and troubleshooting Update the GitHub source pin Choose a full commit SHA from the AIWAF repository and review its SDK changes. Change the x-aiwaf-source Git URL fragment in docker-compose.yml , and the matching io.github.aiwaf.source label in all fifteen runtime Dockerfiles. The assessment proxy shares Express's Dockerfile. If SDK versions changed, update aiwaf.version in the Java/Spring example POMs, source-runner version assertions, and affected JS lockfile metadata or Python dependency locks. Rebuild and recreate the selected services, then run run-source-packages.py --verify-only . Run fresh validation and image scans. Keep older reports identified by source, image and time. A branch name may move; the current full SHA makes source selection reproducible. Source labels are build declarations checked against Compose, not cryptographically signed provenance. run-published-packages.py expects registry versions and is not the source-build runner. Refresh dependencies deliberately python examples/sandbox/lock-python-dependencies.py python examples/sandbox/lock-python-dependencies.py --refresh-build-tools The first command refreshes resolved wheel pins/hashes; the second changes only setuptools/wheel while preserving other pins. Review lock diffs, platform requirements and advisories before rebuilding. Node builds use npm ci ; changing manifests requires matching lockfiles. Base digests and Java/Spring security overrides need explicit updates. A pinned source does not prove all package/image inputs produce bit-for-bit identical outputs. Optional profiles Profile Services Purpose assessment security-fixture, aiwaf-assessment Direct/protected outcome checks on loopback 8090/3020. assessment-tls assessment-tls; use with assessment Caddy direct/protected TLS on loopback 8443/8444. trainer aiwaf-trainer Shared access-log training example; independent of the fifteen-runtime validation. tests aiwaf-tests Optional existing test image; not a replacement for source runner/SDK suites. docker compose --profile assessment stop aiwaf-assessment security-fixture docker compose --profile assessment --profile assessment-tls stop assessment-tls The TLS root/private CA material stays in assessment_tls_data . Export only the public root as described in TLS validation . After a large host clock jump, restart Caddy so it can renew its short-lived leaf certificates. Preserve and inspect state docker compose ps docker compose logs --tail 100 aiwaf-django docker compose exec redis redis-cli INFO keyspace docker compose restart aiwaf-django Normal restarts and docker compose down preserve named volumes. down -v deletes stored state and assessment CA data. Do not use it as a routine remedy for false positives. Global Redis flushing destroys other runtimes' evidence; use fresh synthetic clients and inspect service namespaces first. The isolated outage runner is preferable to stopping shared Redis during a test run. Diagnose a failed check Symptom Check Source/version assertion fails Compare resolved Compose source with image labels. Rebuild and recreate; restarting a container does not install a new image. GitHub fetch or registry install fails Check Docker network/proxy access, repository visibility and the full SHA. Do not silently substitute a sibling checkout. Django or burst requests time out Finish scans/builds, verify application/upstream health, and rerun the affected target alone. Record any timeout change; the matrix default is five seconds. Normal requests are blocked after attacks Inspect persistent reputation and actual forwarded client IPs. Verify namespaces and headers; avoid erasing state to hide false positives. TLS verification fails Use localhost, the exported CA and both assessment profiles; inspect certificate time validity and Caddy logs. Keep certificate verification enabled. Grype is slow on Windows Use Docker's Linux engine and the dedicated database volume, not Windows bind-mounted SQLite storage. Inspect scanner errors; scan failure is not a clean result. PHP blocks ordinary routes Use its separate Composer package and autoloader. Sandbox UUID-only path rules are disabled for Juice Shop. PHP remains outside the current validated source scope. Generated files and cleanup Keep source, Dockerfiles, committed locks, fixtures, tests and the latest evidence. Generated reports, bytecode, dependency directories, tool caches and exported TLS certificates are ignored and excluded from images. Delete only exact obsolete paths after confirming they belong to the sandbox; do not remove package manifests, lockfiles or every JSON file. The stack contains a deliberately vulnerable application and synthetic forwarded-IP controls. Use an isolated evaluation environment. The fixture endpoints bind to loopback; normal proxy ports follow Compose bindings. Production network and trust policies need their own review.

title: OWASP Top 10 coverage
text: Topic guide OWASP Top 10 coverage The OWASP Top 10:2025 describes broad application risks. The sandbox combines request observations, confirmed SQL outcomes, reference-application rules, TLS checks and dependency findings. Those are different kinds of evidence. A passing scenario establishes only its tested outcome. It does not close an entire OWASP category. Evaluate each category against your application, deployment, and current dependency findings. Category-by-category scope 2025 category Implemented checks Remaining scope A01 Broken Access Control Reference cross-user reads/writes, anonymous access, role spoofing, protected-field assignment and CSRF. Production identity, ownership, tenant and egress/SSRF policies. AIWAF does not supply application authorization. A02 Security Misconfiguration Sensitive-file/debug exposure and security response headers on direct/protected fixtures. Host/cloud configuration, CORS, cookies and complete deployment audits. A03 Software Supply Chain Failures Manifest/lock fingerprints, Python wheel hashes, pinned images, npm production audits, Grype JS/Python/Java/OS image scans. High advisories remain; PHP, build provenance, signing, exploitability triage and resolved SBOM verification remain separate. A04 Cryptographic Failures Trusted TLS 1.2/1.3; rejection of old protocols, untrusted roots and wrong hostname; PBKDF2 passwords with independent salts. At-rest encryption, production secrets/key management and application-wide cryptography. A05 Injection Two SQL login payloads per integration with token-issuance assertions and benign controls. Other SQL/XSS/XXE/command/LFI-shaped payloads are observations. No blanket injection pass; browser execution, callbacks and additional backend side-effect assertions are needed for other exploit classes. A06 Insecure Design Negative quantity with no side effects, idempotent replay, conflicting payload under the same key and concurrent inventory budget. Application-owned purchase/refund/workflow rules and resource budgets. A07 Authentication Failures Reference session rotation, expiry, logout/revocation; reset actor binding, expiry and single use; MFA requirement, actor binding and replay rejection. Real identity/MFA/reset providers, delivery and production account/session policies. A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures Original signed reference data accepted; modified subject and forged signature rejected. Package signatures, trusted updates, deserialization and other integrity boundaries. A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures Exactly one correlated redacted failed-login event/alert; modified/truncated history rejected. External SIEM delivery, persistent append-only storage and incident response. A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions Generic injected exception plus recovery; isolated live Express Redis and shared upstream failures; Python cache regressions. Every-runtime outages, production failover, rollback and resource cleanup under broader failures. What the reference fixture proves The fixture is separate from Juice Shop. It uses two users, independently salted PBKDF2-SHA256 hashes with 600,000 iterations, random sessions, test-only reset/MFA controls, isolated inventory and HMAC-protected data. The Compose service starts securely; regression tests also use deliberately broken fixture modes to verify that assertions detect failures. Each check validates response fields and side effects, not merely an HTTP denial. Per-run state is cleaned afterward; fixture signing keys/state are ephemeral. The default control credential is sandbox-assessment-only ; AIWAF_ASSESSMENT_TOKEN overrides it for both Compose and runner. Tokens/passwords are excluded from reports. Reference rules demonstrate an assessment technique, not AIWAF implementations of identity/business policies. Interpret supply-chain findings Run assessment/scan_images.py to scan the fifteen non-PHP images with pinned Grype. Retain image IDs, advisory database metadata, package locations and scan timestamps with your results. A03 image checks fail when high/critical matches exist. Review wont-fix , not-fixed and available fix versions without suppressing findings. Shared packages may produce repeated matches across images; a match count is not a count of distinct exploitable vulnerabilities. A clean npm audit can coexist with OS or other ecosystem findings. Advisory matches require location and exploitability triage. Rebuilt images require matching scan evidence; an older scan does not certify a new image. How to describe a result Identify which scenarios passed, which findings remain, and which controls were not assessed. Avoid “OWASP certified,” “10/10 compliant,” or “all other OWASP categories closed.” Completion of the payload matrix establishes collection of observations without request errors, not universal exploit prevention. See the validation workflow to generate evidence, and application testing to add assertions for your own security boundaries.

Dependency hardening Node: npm ci , compiler build stage, digest-pinned Node 22 slim runtime, npm 12.2.0, patched bundled undici and brace-expansion. Python: refreshed digest-pinned 3.11 base, Linux x86_64/CPython 3.11 wheel hashes, setuptools 84.0.0 and wheel 0.48.0. Java: Jackson 2.22.3; Spring Boot 4.0.8 overrides Jackson 2/3 to 2.22.3/3.1.7 and Tomcat to 11.0.25. Java/R: patched Ubuntu OpenSSL 3.0.13-0ubuntu3.16 packages. Runtime images copy their own application and shared helpers. Tool caches, TLS material, reports and build outputs are excluded from build contexts. These measures reduce known findings; they are not provenance verification or a resolved SBOM. Read remaining advisory findings .

title: Your first sandbox run
text: Tutorial Your first sandbox run You will start Juice Shop, Redis, and fifteen non-PHP proxies, then verify their source versions and test one endpoint. Run every command from the sandbox repository root. 1. Check requirements Docker Desktop using Linux containers, or Docker Engine with BuildKit and Compose additional-context support. Git, Python 3.10+, and network access to GitHub and package registries. Host Node.js only for JavaScript unit tests outside Docker. Time and disk space for Node, Python, Java, and R image builds. docker version docker compose version git --version python --version 2. Clone the sandbox git clone https://github.com/aayushgauba/sandbox.git cd sandbox python -m pip install requests Use a sandbox revision containing run-source-packages.py and the GitHub source contexts. x-aiwaf-source in Compose pins AIWAF commit 843a35f4fd48b4ef565e3c1ec8a42db9b1c41946 . BuildKit clones it automatically. A host SDK installation or adjacent checkout does not select the SDK inside the image. 3. Build the validated integrations docker compose up -d --build aiwaf aiwaf_fastify aiwaf_hapi aiwaf_koa aiwaf_nest aiwaf_next aiwaf_adonis aiwaf_sails aiwaf-django aiwaf-flask aiwaf-fastapi aiwaf-java aiwaf-spring aiwaf-java-r aiwaf-spring-r docker compose ps Compose starts Redis and Juice Shop dependencies. Without a service selection, docker compose up -d --build also starts the default PHP integrations. PHP is outside this validation scope. Checkpoint: Redis and Juice Shop should be healthy and all selected proxies running. The baseline is http://localhost:3001 ; Express protection uses http://localhost:3000 . 4. Verify the installed source python examples/sandbox/run-source-packages.py --verify-only The verifier compares each running proxy's io.github.aiwaf.source label with the resolved Compose context, checks Python/JavaScript 1.1.1 and Java 1.3.2, checks installation paths, and verifies the Java SQL-inspection class. Stale containers fail with a rebuild-required assertion. results_local_versions.json records the installed SDKs under examples/sandbox/ . The filename denotes local Docker execution; github_source identifies remote source and commit. 5. Test a protected endpoint python examples/sandbox/smoke-test.py --target node=http://127.0.0.1:3000 --burst-workers 16 --output examples/sandbox/results_first_smoke.json python examples/sandbox/validate-login-bypass.py --target node=http://127.0.0.1:3000 --output examples/sandbox/results_first_login.json The smoke check requires normal requests to succeed, automation and excess traffic to be denied, and benign invalid credentials to reach Juice Shop as a 401. The SQL check requires two payloads to fail to obtain an authentication token; token values are omitted from reports. Continue with full validation . If a check fails, inspect docker compose logs --tail 100 aiwaf and troubleshooting . ← Overview Validation →

title: Validation and reports
text: How-to guide Validation and reports Run the source validation workflow Start the fifteen integrations from the tutorial , then the optional reference services. Run checks sequentially to avoid build/scan load distorting request timeouts. docker compose --profile assessment up -d --build security-fixture aiwaf-assessment python -m pip install requests python -m unittest discover -s examples/sandbox -p 'test_*.py' node --test examples/sandbox/common/redis-cache.test.js examples/sandbox/common/proxy.test.js python examples/sandbox/run-source-packages.py The runner verifies source labels and versions, then executes smoke, SQL login, payload matrix, post-matrix SQL, reference checks and nine production npm audits: eight proxy trees and the SDK. It excludes PHP. --verify-only performs installed-source checks. --skip-completed accepts prior suite reports only when the recorded source URL/commit matches; omit it for a fresh run. Interpret each check Check What success establishes Limit Smoke Normal/lowercase headers succeed; automation and excess traffic are denied; benign JSON login reaches the app. Not a complete attack evaluation. Burst checks need accepted and denied requests, so blanket blocking fails. SQL login Two SQL payloads cannot issue a token; invalid credentials supply the control. Specific exploit outcomes only. Tokens are omitted. Payload matrix All selected observations complete without request errors. Exit 0 does not mean every payload was denied or every exploit prevented. Reference fixture Status, response fields and state changes enforce each tested application rule. Application-owned controls; an unrelated WAF 403 cannot count as success. npm/image audit Advisory query and matched dependency findings are recorded. Package locations and exploitability still need triage. The legacy attack suite classifies 403/405/409/429 as blocked; these statuses can come from another layer. Default legacy probes can also be rejected by header validation before payload inspection. A block percentage is not a demonstrated detection rate. The newer matrix uses browser headers except in scenarios designed to alter them. Rate-limit and brute-force scenarios retain one public client IP throughout, then generate a fresh IP for the next scenario. Other probes rotate per request. Redis is not flushed, so retained reputation may reveal false positives after attack traffic. Target one runtime or resume observations python examples/sandbox/smoke-test.py --target django=http://127.0.0.1:3009 --burst-workers 16 python examples/sandbox/validate-login-bypass.py --target java=http://127.0.0.1:8080 python examples/sandbox/validate-runtime-matrix.py --exclude laravel --exclude symfony --exclude wordpress --output examples/sandbox/results_local_payload.json The matrix's default per-request timeout is five seconds. --timeout changes that requirement; disclose any change when reporting results. --resume retains saved baselines and targets without errors, and reruns failed targets. Keep resumes within the same source/configuration; the matrix alone does not verify commit provenance. Extended checks with TLS Caddy exposes only loopback ports 8443/8444. Its internal CA stays in a dedicated Docker volume. Export the public root certificate; pass it explicitly to the runner without changing host trust. docker compose --profile assessment --profile assessment-tls up -d --build security-fixture aiwaf-assessment assessment-tls New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force examples/sandbox/assessment/.tls docker compose --profile assessment --profile assessment-tls cp assessment-tls:/data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt examples/sandbox/assessment/.tls/root.crt python examples/sandbox/assessment/run.py --extended --fixture https://localhost:8443 --fixture https://localhost:8444 --ca-file examples/sandbox/assessment/.tls/root.crt --tls-url https://localhost:8443 --tls-url https://localhost:8444 --npm-audit --local-runtime-scope --output examples/sandbox/results_local_owasp_extended.json Tests require trusted TLS 1.2/1.3, rejection of old protocols, untrusted roots and incorrect hostnames. Client-side inability to test an old protocol is not_assessed , not a server pass. Both profiles are needed because TLS depends on the fixture/proxy. Caddy preserves synthetic client IPs for loopback assessment; that trust arrangement is not a production proxy policy. For HTTP-only checks, use both --fixture http://localhost:8090 and --fixture http://localhost:3020 with --extended --allow-local-http . HTTP transport remains unassessed. Omitting --npm-audit leaves the advisory query unassessed. Isolated failures and dependency scans python examples/sandbox/assessment/outages.py python examples/sandbox/audit-published-proxies.py --include-sdk --output examples/sandbox/results_local_npm_audits.json python examples/sandbox/assessment/scan_images.py python examples/sandbox/assessment/render_report.py Outage tests run an isolated Express process with actual Redis/upstream connection refusals. They require generic 503 with no application call for Redis, and generic 502 for upstream failure. They do not stop shared Redis or demonstrate failover in all runtimes. Python outage behavior has separate SDK unit/HTTP regressions. Grype 0.120.0 is pinned by image digest, scans fifteen built images including OS packages, mounts the Docker socket and uses sandbox_grype_db for its advisory database. It exits 1 on high/critical findings or scan errors; lower findings are retained. --service selects images; --resume reuses raw reports only when filesystem layers and runtime configuration match, retaining original scan dates. Report reference Files under examples/sandbox/ Contents results_local_versions.json , results_local_run.json , results_local_validation.md Source runner provenance, suite exits, aggregate validation. Existing reports may describe an earlier run; inspect timestamps/source. results_local_smoke.json , results_local_login*.json , results_local_payload.json Runtime requests, SQL outcomes, matrix observations. results_local_owasp*.json , results_local_outages.json , results_local_npm_audits.json Reference/TLS outcomes, isolated failures and npm audits. results_local_image_advisories.json , results_owasp_scan_*.json Image finding summaries and raw package-location evidence. results_local_owasp_summary.md Category totals, failed image checks, remaining scope and grouped high/critical findings. The report renderer reads the results_local_* files together; it does not reconcile timestamps or source provenance for every component. Generate fresh components before treating an aggregate as current. Reports are ignored by Git and excluded from build images. Assessment statuses are pass , fail , error , and not_assessed . Failures/errors cause exit 1. A clean npm audit can coexist with OS image advisories. OWASP scope explains the remaining work.

title: Testing an AIWAF-protected application
text: Testing an AIWAF-protected application Test both the application's successful responses and the protection decisions that can stop a request before its handler. Start with deterministic limits, then add the full middleware stack and deployment checks. Choose the right test boundary Layer What to verify What it proves Application tests Validation, authentication, business rules, and successful response bodies. The handler behaves correctly when reached. Focused protection tests An allowed request, a rejected request, and a scoped exemption for one enabled check. The middleware is registered and enforces the intended policy. Full application integration Actual middleware order, route manifest, headers, storage, and known model fixtures. The checks work together with your framework and application. Deployment tests Real proxy/client identity, repeated requests across workers, shared state, and health probes. The deployed topology behaves as intended. Keep a successful request beside each rejection assertion. A suite where every request fails can hide a broken registration, missing route, or overly broad policy. The examples below enable only rate limiting so an unrelated header or model check cannot cause an accidental pass. Isolate state before writing assertions Use a fresh application or test client lifecycle and dedicated data, log, and model locations. CSV files and Redis state do not roll back with a database transaction. Give parallel workers separate cache namespaces, databases, or directories. Keep one namespace shared only for tests explicitly checking cross-worker behavior. Use fixed route budgets and an isolated manifest path. A discovered route policy can override the global limit, so test the effective route policy. Keep the client identity stable while testing a bucket. Use a new identity when testing independent clients. Use a known JSON model fixture for anomaly decisions. Do not train on live traffic as part of a deterministic application test. For window expiry tests, control the clock at the component boundary or use a dedicated timed integration test. Avoid long sleeps in ordinary tests. Django's test runner creates test databases, but caches are not automatically isolated or cleared between tests. Use a dedicated test cache before clearing it. See Django's testing overview . Write and run Flask protection tests Create an empty working directory, install aiwaf[flask] , and save this complete file as test_flask_protection.py . It builds a new application and temporary CSV directory for every test, explicitly selects memory counters, and pins both route budgets. python -m pip install "aiwaf[flask]" test_flask_protection.py """Run with: python -m unittest discover -s examples/testing -p test_flask_protection.py -v""" from pathlib import Path import tempfile import unittest from flask import Flask from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF, aiwaf_exempt, aiwaf_exempt_from class ProtectionTests(unittest.TestCase): def setUp(self): # A new application and state directory for every test. directory = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix=".ci-protection-validation-", dir=Path.cwd()) self.addCleanup(directory.cleanup) app = Flask(__name__) app.config.update( TESTING=True, AIWAF_USE_CSV=True, AIWAF_DATA_DIR=directory.name, AIWAF_RATE_CACHE_BACKEND="memory", AIWAF_PATH_MANIFEST=str(Path(directory.name) / "paths.json"), AIWAF_RATE_WINDOW=60, AIWAF_RATE_MAX=3, AIWAF_RATE_FLOOD=100, AIWAF_PATH_RULES=[ {"PREFIX": path, "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}} for path in ("/api/message", "/api/preview") ], ) @app.get("/api/message") def message(): return {"message": "Protected"} @app.get("/health") @aiwaf_exempt def health(): return {"ok": True} @app.get("/api/preview") @aiwaf_exempt_from("rate_limit") def preview(): return {"message": "Preview"} AIWAF(app, middlewares=["rate_limit"]) self.client = app.test_client() def test_protected_route_throttles(self): for _ in range(3): response = self.client.get("/api/message") self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200) self.assertEqual(response.json, {"message": "Protected"}) response = self.client.get("/api/message") self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 429) self.assertEqual(response.json, {"error": "too_many_requests"}) def test_health_stays_available_after_throttling(self): for _ in range(4): self.client.get("/api/message") response = self.client.get("/health") self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200) self.assertEqual(response.json, {"ok": True}) def test_selective_exemption_bypasses_rate_limit(self): self.assertEqual( [self.client.get("/api/preview").status_code for _ in range(5)], [200] * 5, ) if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main() python -m unittest discover -s . -p test_flask_protection.py -v Expect three passing tests. The first verifies three successful responses followed by HTTP 429 and the exact too_many_requests JSON body. The others verify health availability after the protected route is throttled and that a selective rate-limit exemption permits repeated requests. Checkpoint: Change the expected throttle status from 429 to 200 and rerun: that assertion should fail. Restore it afterward. This confirms the test can detect the behavior it claims to check. This fixture exercises AIWAF behavior independently. In your own project, also test your actual app factory and live routes so a mistake in production registration cannot be hidden by a separate fixture. Write and run Django protection tests In a separate empty directory, install aiwaf[django] and save both files below. The fixture uses Django's test client, ORM-backed AIWAF stores, an in-memory SQLite test database, and a dedicated local-memory cache. The URL configuration is the test module itself. python -m pip install "aiwaf[django]" django_test_settings.py """Settings for this standalone example, separate from your application's settings.""" from pathlib import Path SECRET_KEY = "local-documentation-test-key" INSTALLED_APPS = ["aiwaf.django"] DATABASES = {"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3", "NAME": ":memory:"}} DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD = "django.db.models.BigAutoField" # Only for this standalone fixture: create AIWAF tables without generated migrations. MIGRATION_MODULES = {"aiwaf": None} ROOT_URLCONF = "test_django_protection" ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["testserver"] MIDDLEWARE = ["aiwaf.django.middleware.RateLimitMiddleware"] CACHES = { "default": { "BACKEND": "django.core.cache.backends.locmem.LocMemCache", "LOCATION": "documentation-protection-tests", } } AIWAF_USE_CSV = False AIWAF_PATH_MANIFEST = str(Path(__file__).with_name("unused-test-manifest.json")) AIWAF_RATE_WINDOW = 60 AIWAF_RATE_MAX = 3 AIWAF_RATE_FLOOD = 100 AIWAF_EXEMPT_PATHS = ["/health"] AIWAF_SETTINGS = { "PATH_RULES": [ {"PREFIX": "/api/message", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}}, {"PREFIX": "/api/preview", "DISABLE": ["rate_limit"]}, ] } test_django_protection.py """Run from this directory using django_test_settings; see /docs/testing.""" from django.core.cache import cache from django.http import JsonResponse from django.test import TestCase from django.urls import path def message(request): return JsonResponse({"message": "Protected"}) def health(request): return JsonResponse({"ok": True}) def preview(request): return JsonResponse({"message": "Preview"}) urlpatterns = [ path("api/message", message), path("health", health), path("api/preview", preview), ] class ProtectionTests(TestCase): def setUp(self): # django_test_settings points only at a dedicated local-memory test cache. cache.clear() self.addCleanup(cache.clear) def test_protected_route_throttles(self): for _ in range(3): response = self.client.get("/api/message") self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200) self.assertEqual(response.json(), {"message": "Protected"}) response = self.client.get("/api/message") self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 429) self.assertEqual(response.json(), {"error": "too_many_requests"}) def test_health_stays_available_after_throttling(self): for _ in range(4): self.client.get("/api/message") response = self.client.get("/health") self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200) self.assertEqual(response.json(), {"ok": True}) def test_selective_exemption_bypasses_rate_limit(self): self.assertEqual( [self.client.get("/api/preview").status_code for _ in range(5)], [200] * 5, ) python -m django test test_django_protection --settings=django_test_settings -v 2 Expect three passing tests and creation/destruction of the test database. TestCase isolates ORM changes; setUp() and cleanup clear only the dedicated local-memory cache. The standalone fixture disables AIWAF migrations to create its tables directly. In an existing project, keep your real migrations, include AIWAF in INSTALLED_APPS , and run your application's tests with its dedicated test settings. Adapt these assertions to the routes from the Django setup guide . Keep another suite using your real ROOT_URLCONF and complete MIDDLEWARE list: this focused fixture intentionally exercises only the rate limiter. Django route-policy detail This fixture uses AIWAF_EXEMPT_PATHS for health and a PATH_RULES entry disabling only rate_limit for preview. In the current source, the rate limiter runs before Django resolves the view, while decorator detection reads request.resolver_match . A selective decorator alone did not bypass the limiter in this full test-client request. Use the explicit path policy for this case, and test decorators through your actual middleware stack. Apply the same assertions to other frameworks The status sequence and test structure above belong to these Python fixtures. For other runtimes, use that runtime's configuration names, response contract, and policy precedence. FastAPI: use its test client against the actual ASGI application. Keep the client in a context manager when startup/shutdown initializes resources. Give each test its own policy/state configuration; see the FastAPI setup guide . Node.js: create a fresh app and AIWAF middleware instance per test. Use the framework's injection facility or an HTTP client against an ephemeral local port. Verify a normal response, configured throttle/block response, and exemption. See Node.js operations . Java: test the engine decision independently, then exercise the registered Spring filter or Servlet filter through your framework test harness. Keep shared Redis integration tests separate from memory-backed tests. See Java operations . Expand to the full protection stack Headers and parsing: pair valid browser/API requests with requests violating your configured requirements. Assert the rejection reason or body as well as status. Exemptions: verify that the intended check is bypassed and that another enabled check still runs. The rate-only examples prove the bypass, but do not prove other checks remain active. Flood and reputation: distinguish a soft throttle from a hard block. Verify persistent state and later requests separately using disposable storage. Models: cover a known normal sample, a known anomaly, and missing/invalid model handling for your configured runtime. Keep training tests separate from inference tests. Route discovery: generate the manifest from the test application's live route table, verify the protected route is present, and repeat the behavior assertions with the manifest loaded. Observation: check the expected log record and response status, including denied requests, without relying on a production log file. For Redis or multiple workers, send a combined request sequence across workers using the same client identity and bucket. Assert the aggregate budget, expiry behavior, and configured backend-failure behavior. A single-process in-memory test cannot establish those guarantees. Run the examples in continuous integration From the AIWAF website checkout, the checked-in examples run with these commands. Install the relevant framework extras first. python -m unittest discover -s examples/testing -p test_flask_protection.py -v cd examples/testing python -m django test test_django_protection --settings=django_test_settings -v 2 Run application and focused protection tests on each change. Run shared-backend and deployed-topology checks in a separate integration job with disposable services. Save failure output and effective policy configuration so failures can be reproduced locally. Diagnose a failing protection test Failure Check next Expected 429, got 200 Middleware registration, route/IP exemptions, effective manifest rules, changing client identity, and counters split across workers. First request already rejected Leaked cache/blocklist state, missing required headers, route mismatch, or another enabled check. Passes alone, fails in the suite Shared storage/cache keys, module-level app reuse, test order, and model/manifest files left by another test. Expected JSON, got HTML or a redirect Wrong URL, trailing-slash routing, framework exception handling, or a response produced by the application/proxy. Use the Redis-enabled multi-runtime sandbox for pinned GitHub source builds and cross-runtime checks. Follow the first-run tutorial , run SQL, TLS, outage and dependency checks , and review OWASP coverage and limits before interpreting results. Continue with troubleshooting , configuration reference , and state ownership across workers .

title: Troubleshooting and Verification
text: Troubleshooting and Verification CLI rejects --app app.py --app takes a Python import target, not a filename. For app.py containing app = Flask(__name__) , run from its directory: aiwaf init --framework flask --app app:app For a factory use app:create_app . For Django use --framework django --settings project.settings . Install dependencies and load the application's configuration in the same environment; discovery imports the live application. Manifest has only / and static routes Confirm the imported file is your intended application, all blueprints/routers are registered, and the app factory finishes before discovery: python -c "import app; print(app.__file__); print(*sorted(r.rule for r in app.app.url_map.iter_rules()), sep='\n')" This diagnostic is for a Flask module-level app. Regenerate the manifest after registering additional routes. An unimported blueprint cannot appear in the live route table. Website setup page returns 404 or 500 /docs/python/setup redirects to /docs/python/setup/django . /python/setup/django redirects to the same canonical guide. Both app runners register the shared documentation blueprint. Unknown pages return 404; errors inside an existing template remain server errors. Check which checkout the WSGI worker imports and which entrypoint the host uses. Deploy documentation.py and all templates together, including shared includes. Reload the host's web application or restart workers after updating source/dependencies. Read the server traceback for import errors, missing includes, or initialization failures. A 500 page alone does not identify the cause. python -m unittest discover -s tests -v python -c "from wsgi import application; print(application.url_map)" curl -i https://aiwaf.org/health The import check initializes the actual website and may create runtime files. Tests isolate documentation routing and rendering; a passing test does not establish that the deployed worker has reloaded. /health is liveness, not database/cache readiness. Normal traffic is blocked, or test traffic is never blocked Compare response details and logs with the selected middleware, route plan, client IP, headers, and block/reputation state. A 403 may come from AIWAF or a proxy; avoid attributing it without evidence. Rate throttling can have different status semantics from a deterministic block. Private clients, health paths, static paths, or route annotations may be exempt. Local curl success alone does not demonstrate protection for public clients. To exercise header validation, use a non-exempt route and a client context matching deployment; include representative User-Agent/Accept headers and browser-standard headers such as Accept-Language/Accept-Encoding in the normal case. Plain curl requests can be rejected by the website's header policy; use a browser or matching headers to check protected documentation. The website explicitly exempts /health for liveness probes. Configure a small staging threshold and test below, at, and above the boundary. Do not disable protection globally to resolve a single route. Client IP or multi-worker counters look wrong Inspect address extraction for your adapter and the actual forwarding-header chain. Have the trusted outer proxy overwrite client-supplied headers. Java has explicit trusted proxy CIDRs; Python/Node resolution follows their own rules. File persistence is separate from a shared rate cache. Redis configuration must resolve to an active shared backend. In Flask, Redis initialization can fall back to memory; test enforcement across two workers and examine initialization logs. Use the same rate-key prefix for workers sharing one service, and distinct prefixes for unrelated services. Training produces no usable model Verify that the trainer reads the actual log path/format, logs include response observations, minimum sample thresholds are met, and the output model is written where runtime inference loads it. Representative normal traffic is needed; forced training does not repair missing or malformed inputs. Inspect trainer/model help for the installed adapter: aiwaf flask train --help aiwaf flask model --help # Django uses its management commands: python manage.py detect_and_train --help Python requires JSON model state. Regenerate legacy executable artifacts rather than renaming their extension. Verify model load diagnostics after deployment/reload. Models with different feature schemas or native formats need a supported conversion path or retraining. Verification before publishing documentation Render every page; check internal links, fragment anchors, setup redirects, and unknown-page behavior. Then test code samples with the installed runtime in a clean staging environment, including a normal request and an intentional rejection. Finally test the public URLs after deployment. These are separate checks. See configuration , migration , and the runtime operations pages for the exact settings and supported tools.

title: Create your first protected app
text: First protected app / Step 2 of 6 Create your first protected app In the directory you prepared, create a file named app.py . This is a complete application. You can copy the whole block without filling in missing routes or configuration. 1. Create app.py app.py """Local learning app. Its small limits are for the tutorial, not production.""" from flask import Flask from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF, aiwaf_exempt app = Flask(__name__) app.config.update( AIWAF_USE_CSV=True, AIWAF_DATA_DIR="aiwaf_data", AIWAF_RATE_WINDOW=60, AIWAF_RATE_MAX=3, AIWAF_RATE_FLOOD=100, AIWAF_PATH_RULES=[ {"PREFIX": "/api/message", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}}, ], AIWAF_LOG_DIR="aiwaf_logs", AIWAF_LOG_FORMAT="json", ) @app.get("/api/message") def message(): return {"message": "Hello from a protected route"} @app.get("/health") @aiwaf_exempt def health(): return {"ok": True} AIWAF(app, middlewares=["rate_limit", "logging"]) 2. Understand the pieces Flask(__name__) creates the application object. It is named app , so both Flask and the AIWAF CLI will use the import target app:app . app.config.update(...) applies settings before middleware registration. The teaching limit is three requests in 60 seconds; the flood threshold is intentionally higher so the rate-limit demonstration does not create a flood block. AIWAF_PATH_RULES pins the message route to the teaching budget. Generated manifests can supply inferred rate settings; the explicit rule keeps this exercise at three requests. /api/message is the protected route. The handler runs only when the selected middleware allows the request. @aiwaf_exempt marks /health as exempt from protection. Use this deliberately for liveness; it does not turn off checks for other routes. AIWAF(...) registers rate limiting and logging after the routes have been defined. Header, keyword, geo, and anomaly checks are not selected in this teaching app, making the first verification predictable with a plain HTTP client. Selected checks are a learning choice The app demonstrates two components. It is not a complete production security policy. The framework setup and architecture guides explain all , auto , and the other checks. 3. Start the development server python -m flask --app app:app run --port 5000 The console should report a development server listening at http://127.0.0.1:5000 . Leave that terminal open. Flask's development server is suitable for this local exercise; choose your framework's production server before deployment. 4. Recognize the generated files aiwaf-demo/ app.py .venv/ aiwaf_logs/ # request logs aiwaf_data/ # CSV state when a store needs it .aiwaf/ # route manifest after the next step Runtime directories are created as they are needed. Keep the application source in Git; ignore the virtual environment, request logs, local state, and generated route manifest. Checkpoint Your server starts from app.py without Redis or a trained anomaly model. Do not send repeated requests yet; the verification chapter starts with a fresh counter. Previous: Prepare your environment Next: Discover your routes

title: Prepare your environment
text: First protected app / Step 1 of 6 Prepare your environment This tutorial builds a small Flask API and follows one request from the client through AIWAF to the handler and request log. You will see three successful requests followed by a rate-limit response, and then exempt one route without removing protection from the others. Before you begin Use Python 3.11 or newer, a terminal, and an empty directory. The commands use the current Python AIWAF API. They do not require Redis, Rust, a trained model, or the AIWAF source checkout. Flask is the teaching example; use the framework guides if you are integrating an existing app. 1. Create a workspace mkdir aiwaf-demo cd aiwaf-demo python -m venv .venv A virtual environment keeps the tutorial's packages separate from other applications. Run every later command from this directory with that environment active. 2. Activate the environment Linux and macOS source .venv/bin/activate Windows PowerShell .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 If your machine names Python python3 or uses the py launcher, use that command to create the environment. Once active, python should refer to its interpreter. 3. Install the framework extra python -m pip install "aiwaf[flask]" python -m pip show aiwaf Flask The flask extra installs the dependencies for the Flask adapter. aiwaf-rust is optional acceleration and is deliberately left out of this first walkthrough. You can add it after you have verified the baseline behavior. 4. Check the import python -c "from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF; print('Flask adapter ready')" Flask adapter ready If the import fails, compare python -m pip --version with the active interpreter. Do not install packages into a different environment to silence the error. Checkpoint You have an isolated environment and can import the Flask adapter. No server or model is running yet. title: Read logs and plan training
text: First protected app / Step 6 of 6 Read logs and plan training Enforcement decisions are easier to operate when you can connect them to request observations. The tutorial already selects logging; now inspect the files it writes and understand the boundary between logging and training. 1. Read the access log From the app directory: python -c "from pathlib import Path; print(Path('aiwaf_logs/access.log').read_text())" AIWAF_LOG_FORMAT='json' writes JSON records to the access log. Look for the request path and response status for the message/preview calls. Timestamps, durations, addresses, and record details depend on the runtime; the file is evidence of the observed requests, not a trained model. 2. Separate three kinds of state Data Purpose Tutorial behavior Rate counters Decide whether the current request crosses the window In memory in this process; lost on restart Request logs / CSV state Record observations and persist store data when used Files under the configured directories Model artifact Score behavior after offline training No anomaly model is trained or selected here Keeping CSV files does not make rate counters shared across workers. See shared state configuration before scaling beyond a single process. 3. Inspect the trainer before running it aiwaf flask train --help aiwaf flask model --help For an application with a representative combined-format log corpus, the Flask trainer accepts: aiwaf flask train --log-dir /path/to/combined-format-logs This is a separate operational example, not the next command to run on these few JSON tutorial records. Check the installed trainer's supported input formats, volume thresholds, output path, and model diagnostics. Convert or collect a supported log format deliberately; do not assume the logger format is the trainer format. Current Python persisted models use JSON. A file with a different extension does not become a compatible model by renaming it. Collect representative traffic, train with the runtime's supported workflow, and verify model loading before enabling anomaly inference. Logs can contain request data; configure retention and redaction for your application. 4. Choose your next task Integrate the wider Flask middleware set . Follow policy, deterministic checks, observations, and training through the architecture . Configure defaults, exemptions, and a shared backend . Operate Python training and state . Upgrade an existing installation . Checkpoint You can locate request observations, distinguish them from counters/models, and identify what must be verified before a production rollout. title: Add a route policy
text: First protected app / Step 5 of 6 Add a route policy A route policy lets you change one check on one route. Here you will add a preview endpoint that bypasses rate limiting while the existing message endpoint retains its limit. 1. Import the selective exemption helper Change the AIWAF import at the top of app.py: from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF, aiwaf_exempt, aiwaf_exempt_from 2. Add the preview route Insert this handler before the final AIWAF(app, ...) registration: @app.get("/api/preview") @aiwaf_exempt_from("rate_limit") def preview(): return {"message": "Preview has no rate limit"} Also add this explicit preview budget before the final AIWAF registration. It keeps the baseline at three requests even after manifest inference, so five successful requests demonstrate the decorator exemption: # Pin the preview budget too; its decorator selectively bypasses that check. app.config["AIWAF_PATH_RULES"].append( {"PREFIX": "/api/preview", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}} ) The Flask route decorator is outside the AIWAF decorator. aiwaf_exempt_from disables the named check on this handler, while aiwaf_exempt on health marks a full exemption. The example selects rate limiting and logging; adding other checks later requires reviewing the preview route's intended policy. 3. Regenerate and restart aiwaf init --framework flask --app app:app python -m flask --app app:app run --port 5000 Stop the earlier server before starting another one. Run the four-request message test again: its fourth request should still be 429. Then request preview five times: python -c "from urllib.request import urlopen; print([urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/preview').status for _ in range(5)])" [200, 200, 200, 200, 200] Using a different path gives a different default rate bucket; five successes exceed the three-request threshold and demonstrate the selective exemption. Complete app after this change Show the final app.py app.py """Local learning app. Its small limits are for the tutorial, not production.""" from flask import Flask from aiwaf.flask import AIWAF, aiwaf_exempt, aiwaf_exempt_from app = Flask(__name__) app.config.update( AIWAF_USE_CSV=True, AIWAF_DATA_DIR="aiwaf_data", AIWAF_RATE_WINDOW=60, AIWAF_RATE_MAX=3, AIWAF_RATE_FLOOD=100, AIWAF_PATH_RULES=[ {"PREFIX": "/api/message", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}}, ], AIWAF_LOG_DIR="aiwaf_logs", AIWAF_LOG_FORMAT="json", ) @app.get("/api/message") def message(): return {"message": "Hello from a protected route"} @app.get("/health") @aiwaf_exempt def health(): return {"ok": True} # Added in the tutorial's route-policy chapter. @app.get("/api/preview") @aiwaf_exempt_from("rate_limit") def preview(): return {"message": "Preview has no rate limit"} # Pin the preview budget too; its decorator selectively bypasses that check. app.config["AIWAF_PATH_RULES"].append( {"PREFIX": "/api/preview", "RATE_LIMIT": {"WINDOW": 60, "MAX": 3, "FLOOD": 100}} ) AIWAF(app, middlewares=["rate_limit", "logging"]) Checkpoint Message remains limited, preview skips rate limiting, and health keeps its deliberate full exemption. title: Discover your routes
text: First protected app / Step 3 of 6 Discover your routes Route discovery records the routes your application actually registers. It does not create handlers or launch a permanent server. AIWAF can use the generated manifest when building route policy. 1. Import the live application Open a second terminal in aiwaf-demo , activate the same environment, and run: aiwaf init --framework flask --app app:app app:app means “import the module app.py, then read its app object.” A file path such as --app app.py is invalid. If your application uses a factory, use its import target, such as app:create_app . 2. Inspect the manifest python -m json.tool .aiwaf/paths.json You should see a JSON document with schema metadata and a routes collection containing /api/message and /health . Flask's static route may also appear. Counts and context hashes depend on the registered application; they are not fixed tutorial constants. Discovery can change effective policy The manifest includes inferred protections, not just path names. An API route may receive a suggested rate budget such as 120 requests per minute. The explicit /api/message rule in app.py takes precedence for that same prefix, keeping the tutorial limit at three. Review inferred settings before using a generated manifest in an existing app. 3. Check the imported route table If your routes are missing, inspect the module the command is loading: python -c "import app; print(app.__file__); print(*sorted(r.rule for r in app.app.url_map.iter_rules()), sep='\n')" The file should be the app.py you just created, and the route list should include both handlers. An unregistered blueprint or a different module named app cannot contribute the intended routes. 4. Know when to regenerate Regenerate after adding, removing, or changing routes. Restart the development server after generation so later requests use the updated manifest. CLI discovery imports your app and requires its dependencies and configuration to be available. Checkpoint .aiwaf/paths.json contains your live routes, and you know how to verify the import target. Previous: Create your first protected app Next: Verify a rate limit

title: Verify a rate limit
text: First protected app / Step 4 of 6 Verify a rate limit A successful response tells you the handler ran. To verify enforcement, also cross the configured boundary and inspect the response AIWAF returns before the handler. 1. Start with a fresh counter Stop the server with Ctrl+C and start it again: python -m flask --app app:app run --port 5000 The tutorial uses a process-local rate cache, so restarting clears its counters. Keep one development server running and send requests from one client. A production shared cache has a different lifetime. 2. Send four requests Create a file named verify.py beside app.py with the code below. It uses Python's standard library, so it works without curl and does not need browser headers for the tutorial's selected checks. verify.py """Run against a fresh tutorial server on port 5000.""" from urllib.error import HTTPError from urllib.request import urlopen for number in range(1, 5): try: with urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/message") as response: print(number, response.status, response.read().decode().strip()) except HTTPError as response: print(number, response.code, response.read().decode().strip()) with urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:5000/health") as response: print("health", response.status, response.read().decode().strip()) python verify.py For a fresh counter, the statuses should be: 1 200 {"message":"Hello from a protected route"} 2 200 {"message":"Hello from a protected route"} 3 200 {"message":"Hello from a protected route"} 4 429 {"error":"too_many_requests"} Whitespace in JSON may differ. The fourth request is throttled; it does not execute the message handler. This is a rate-limit response, not an anomaly-model prediction or a permanent blacklist entry. 3. Check the exempt route python -c "from urllib.request import urlopen; r=urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:5000/health'); print(r.status, r.read().decode())" 200 {"ok":true} The health handler remains reachable even while the message route is throttled. Wait for the 60-second window to expire, or restart this local teaching app, before repeating the message test. If your result differs First request is already 429: earlier requests used the same bucket; wait for the window or restart the local app. Every request returns 200: verify middleware selection, the loaded app file, the path, explicit route overrides, manifest-inferred budgets, and exemptions. Another running server may be answering on port 5000. You see 403: this tutorial does not select header/keyword checks. Check for different configuration, persisted blocks, or an upstream WAF. Connection refused: check that the first terminal is still running and the port matches. Checkpoint You have observed both a permitted handler response and an enforced rate boundary.
